A key highlight of the programme was the startup and student exhibition, which showcased innovative and locally rooted products, including offerings around makhana—reflecting the potential of combining regional strengths with entrepreneurship and innovation.

🌾 Showcasing innovation rooted in local opportunities such as makhana

Continuing from last year's post: have you ever noticed the "Renunciation Industry"?

Many people have moved into the social sector from the corporate world. Some boast that they bring unique skills and best practices. What they mostly bring is access to capital and the false pride of saviour syndrome. You notice it within five minutes. A room of introductions, mostly middle-aged men, mostly corporate résumés. One of them keeps returning to the past. The role he played. The package he walked away from. The years he is now giving to something bigger than himself. Giving back, he calls it. The audience nods politely. Most of them have been doing this work for thirty years. Then the deference begins, because he has access to money. And somewhere between the deference and the second cup of coffee, he starts dictating terms.

That is the part worth examining.

Money is a qualification for allocating money. It is not a qualification for anything else. It does not teach you how a smallholder sequences a crop cycle against an unreliable monsoon. It does not tell you why a community health worker is trusted in one hamlet and ignored in the next. It does not tell you why only women toil under the scorching sun on that small farm. It does not give you the standing to redesign a farming practice you first heard of last quarter.

The person across the table has spent twenty years learning what does not work. You have spent twenty minutes learning what sounds good, from a consultant whose livelihood depends on the fee you are paying him.

So, for the newly arrived:

1 - The sector was here before you, built by people who never had a glorious career to renounce.

2 - Sacrifice is not a credential. Nobody is auditing your suffering. It appears in no results framework.

3 - Altruism that requires an audience is positioning with a conscience attached.

Close the old book. Nobody here is grading your past. Write the cheque. Ask the questions. Then sit down and listen to the answers. Come to learn and contribute. Not to rule.

#SkinInTheGame

Romanticism or Opportunism - Both won’t solve real problems. Grit Might.
***
Many aspire to join the development sector to “give back.” Some come with emotional romanticism — a heartfelt desire to do good. Others arrive with strategic intent — polishing resumes, building networks, or easing into retirement with a sense of social purpose.

There's nothing wrong with aspiration. But if it’s not grounded in commitment, humility, and a willingness to do the hard work, it’s just romanticism or opportunism. Over the years, I’ve met two familiar archetypes among those wanting to transition into the sector:

The accomplished leader - financially secure, professionally satisfied, and ready to “give back” by offering money, strategy, mentoring, or business wisdom. Most importantly - demonstrates skin in the game.

The corporate drifter — mid-career, no longer in the reckoning for top roles, looking for work-life balance, viewing the development sector as a slower-paced second inning with a fat pay cheque.

To both, I offer a word of caution: this isn’t a place for passive advisors or part-time philosophers. If you’re unwilling to start as a learner, unlearn old habits, and earn credibility through hands-on work, you may struggle to fit in.

The development sector is not a space for lateral entry. It’s not built for those seeking career insulation or intellectual indulgence. It’s built by doers — often young, under-resourced, and uncompromisingly mission-driven — who chose to be here from day one, not as a fallback, but as a calling.

At Social Alpha, we work with those who want to build—not boast. These are innovators who wake up every day wanting to solve real problems for people and the planet. These are professionals who are driven not by applause but by outcomes. They are collaborators who bring expertise, yes, but also empathy and the willingness to work alongside communities, not above them.

If you’re ready to learn, do, and commit — there’s space for you in this journey. But come not with entitlement. Come with energy, purpose, and the humility to start where the impact happens — on the ground.

It's because real change doesn’t begin on a panel. It starts at the last mile.

We were pleased to welcome Dr. Robert Speight, Science Digital Lead, CSIRO (Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation), Australia, to Venture Center for an engaging exchange on industrial biotechnology innovation and startup ecosystems in India and Australia.

Dr. Speight oversees the development of Sciansa, an agentic co-scientist platform, and explores the frontiers of AI for Science research — bringing a valuable perspective to discussions at the intersection of science, technology and innovation. He was previously the Director of the CSIRO Advanced Engineering Biology Future Science Platform from 2022 to 2026.

The visit included an overview of the Venture Center ecosystem, the Early Translation Accelerator and Leap Global Accelerator programs, a tour of our facilities, and discussions on potential areas of collaboration.

The conversations explored Australia’s biotech and biomedical clusters and support mechanisms, India’s growing industrial biotech landscape, the contributions of startups and industry, emerging investment trends, and opportunities for cross-border technology translation and collaboration.

We were also delighted to share Candid 1.0 and Candid 2.0, books capturing stories and insights from Venture Center’s ecosystem, as a small memento of the visit. 

Overall, it was a meaningful exchange, opening new avenues for collaboration between the vibrant biotech ecosystems of India and Australia!
